utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Perhaps I meanwhile briefly address the following matter. The Chamber has pointed out to the Defence the safe conduct orders that it has issued in this case, that: First, such orders are not meant to grant immunity to witnesses for acts committed after leaving their state of residence; and two, that there is no basis for ordering the Prosecution to refrain from contacting witnesses prior to the commencement or after the completion of their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber therefore wonders why the Defence continues to make these requests in its motions for safe conduct. We'd like to hear whether there is any good reason for that, but let it be clear that it is the final reminder of the Chamber on this matter. Good morning, Mr. Javoric. Mr. Javoric, Mr. Lukic will continue his re-examination but only after I have reminded you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Javoric. We'll go through this quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need on our screens P2871, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Javoric, on the screen you will see the minutes of the 4th Session of the Council for National Defence of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. It was held on 15 May 1992. You were there as well. I would like to ask you about that body. I can see that that body issued conclusions. Were those conclusions binding?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Council for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, or was it just a council?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a council that gave proposals to the assembly about many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we're going to look at another document, but let's first pay attention to the first conclusion in this document. It says here the draft of the decision on the organisation and functioning of the Crisis Staff is approved under the proviso that a representative of the garrison in Prijedor be added to the proposed list of the Crisis Staff members. The document was issued on the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up P04086.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are going to look at the decision on the appointment of the Prijedor Crisis Staff. You will see that at the bottom of the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we are on a good page in English. Let's look at the last two lines in the B/C/S version, under the Roman numeral I.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here: "The following are hereby appointed to the post of President, Vice-President, and members of Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in B/C/S, we need to go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we can see a list of a total of ten people. Among the ten people -- we will not read their names aloud. You can do that for yourself. Do you see a representative of the Prijedor garrison among those ten people?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. He's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, the conclusion that we saw and that was passed five days before the decision on the appointment of the Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff was not taken into account, it was not implemented; right? Was that normal? Was it normal for the conclusions by the council to be either implemented or not, as the case may have been?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I would have known nothing about the whole matter, carefully listening to your question tells me exactly what answer you are seeking. That is what we call leading, and you should refrain from that. And it's not the first time that I say it, and I repeat to say it because what you are doing, you're diminishing the probative value of the answers of the witness, and that's something, I think, would not be in your interest. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, did that body, the Council for National Defence of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, did it have the power to issue orders?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that moment. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in the military, based on the decisions of this body?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. I was a member of the military. I was not in the Crisis Staff, nor was anybody from the military a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff is a different body. We are talking about the council.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 3145 of our transcript, lines 17 onwards, you were asked whether you knew that the military police were in Keraterm. You said no. And now I would like to ask you this: Did you know that the Keraterm facility was actually a prison for the Serb soldiers who violated the law?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that but I was not in Keraterm during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Leading, again. I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How would else I ask if he knew?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was Keraterm used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- and don't be upset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't be upset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you can, in follow-up questions, take a course on trial techniques, Mr. Lukic, and you'll learn a lot. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And please correct the transcript reference for the transcript of yesterday. It can't be the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have 3145, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is wrong. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday we -- we are far beyond 3000 transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have been at 31000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 3100, I will correct that. Obviously I have one number less than I should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked by my learned friend whether you knew about the goings-on in the investigation centres. You said that you were never in any of them. What you knew about them, how did you learn all that?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that I went to the corridor, and the connection between the troops and the officers on the corridor and the garrison was regular. And we learned from the intelligence officers what was going on. One of them was Miso Rodic. Radomir and Dragan Radakovic were those who sent us reports. So that's how we knew what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 31456 of yesterday's transcripts, lines 2 through 6, you were asked whether you knew that the VRS shelled Hambarine. Did you ever learn if there was any fighting going on in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said that there was an attack on JNA members near Hambarine. There was an ultimatum to surrender weapons. Weapons were not surrendered. When I gave my statement over a year ago, and you were there, just for one day -- and that was not fair. You should have given me more time to give you that statement. I gave you that statement, you took it, I didn't see it then. I wanted to give you as much information as possible. Subsequently I learned that it was a Lieutenant-Colonel Jakov Maric who ordered the shelling. I didn't know. I didn't see. That's what you can find in my statement. I only learned about that subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you whether you learnt that on the following day there was fighting going on in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 314556 [as interpreted], lines 13 to 16, you were asked whether the VRS had shelled Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have my statement in front of me. Should I have it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't be a bad idea for you to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can repeat the transcript reference you made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you count all pages together, then you have the right number of digits. One less at the beginning and now one in addition. Mr. Lukic, please don't be disturbed. It was just a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but I have to check it and I'll come back to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know, Mr. Javoric, who is the first person who was killed in Kozarac? Do you know that? On that day when fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a JNA soldier, Ranko Zgonjanin's son. He was a younger son, and he was in the military column when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, were there any fightings going on in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just make a correction. [In English] For the transcript, the correct page I quoted wrongly at the beginning is 31450. I apologise. [Interpretation] And now let's go to transcript page 31459, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You wanted to say something about Gornja and Donja Ljubija because you thought that we would be interested. Would you please tell us what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. In Ljubija, Mehmed Topic, who was a Muslim, captain first class, in Ljeskare, Stipo Tokmadzic [phoen], who was a Croat. Owing to those two and some others, there were no paramilitaries in Ljubija. Ljeskare is a mixed village composed of Croats, Muslims, and some Serbs. Donja Ljubija, all Muslims. And owing to those people, the few paramilitaries there were there were disarmed, their weapons were handed over to the barracks, there were no operations there, there was no destruction there, and a lot of the villagers of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity joined the VRS. And now I can give you another sentence, or perhaps two. In Donja Puharska. I can give you a list of people who were not armed at all. Amaragic [phoen], for example, Basic, and so on and so forth. When the police embarked on an operation to disarm paramilitaries where there were no weapons, those houses were not touched. If there were weapons in the houses, there were casualties there. In Hambarine, only a day later in Puharska on a regular patrol they captured Captain Brdo, the assistant for morale affairs. Somebody wanted to cause an incident. It was in Hambarine. After what had happened, they captured those officers and they took away their weapons. I called some officers. The weapons were returned, but the resistance continued even after that for houses where there were arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to thank the Presiding Judge for having allowed me to expand on some topics. I apologise for taking up some valuable time, but I wanted to make sure that the Prosecution understands things properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Javoric, I would have one question. But let me first find exactly the transcript passage dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Javoric, you said that you -- when asked about the attack on Hambarine and who ordered the shelling, you said: "Well, when I gave the statement, it was only one day. I learned later," if I understood you well, "who had ordered that." Whereas, of course, in your statement you say that you do not know who ordered it; although, yesterday you said, well, it was VRS shelling. Before you came to this courtroom, did you have an opportunity to tell Mr. Lukic what you learned meanwhile and what would have changed your statement if you would have known that a year before? Did you have an opportunity to talk to him?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before I arrived, I learned who had carried out the shelling, and I said it clear and loud yesterday: Lieutenant-Colonel Jakov Maric, who was the chief of artillery. He was the only one who could have done that. And when I spoke to Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was interested in, yes. What did you then -- did you speak with Mr. Lukic about it?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was too late to change anything. I arrived on Saturday from the airport. This is my first appearance at any court, let alone such a high tribunal. And if I'd known that things could be changed, that there was a procedure in place for that, I would have done it gladly. I thought I couldn't. But now I've told you everything I know. I wanted to complete the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. Well, at the same time you attested to your own statement in which one reads that you did not know who ordered it. So later, indeed, you told us that it was VRS shelling, and even now you told us that you know who ordered it. But yesterday you attested that the whole of your statement was the truth and nothing but the truth, although you knew at that time that at least in this respect the statement was not correct any further because you, meanwhile, had learned who had ordered that shelling. And you were asked whether you would give the same answers if the same questions would be put to you, and you said yes. Although --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "mostly." I added the word "mostly." If you will allow me, I said who was it who had done the shelling, but I don't know who issued the order to him. I don't know that to this very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Are there any other matters in your statement where you say, "Well, I learned" -- not something in addition, but "I learned something which I denied knowledge of in my statement" or "I learned that what I said in this statement is not accurate"? I am not asking you to add anything, new information you've gained. But what is in your statement, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why did you gain the impression that you couldn't change anything if -- I may take it that Mr. Lukic told you: "Read carefully, and if there is anything which is not accurate, then tell me." I take it that that's what he did.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the procedure and the technology. I thought it was too late to do things. I didn't know that. I'm really being honest. I'm not a professional. I thought that I couldn't change a thing. I don't see a reason why I would not ask you to enter that piece of information. I thought it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Judge Fluegge may have one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Javoric, I have to take you back to an issue we discussed at length yesterday. This is your promotion. You told us yesterday that you had been promoted in December 1992. Can you just briefly describe how this promotion was carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me administrative things. I'm an officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you -- no, no --

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop. You said you were promoted in December 1992. Can you explain what your experience -- from your point of view what happened in December 1992 with respect to your promotion? I'm not asking about what other people did. What you observed and experienced.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the paper in April the following year, on the 17th of April if I'm not mistaken. That is when I was informed. Now when the order arrived to the District Staff from the Main Staff, well, that's for personnel services. I'd just receive information. I have nothing to do with any of that, how all of that went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This clarifies the matter. That means in December 1992, you were not informed about your promotion at all?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have been because it is written retroactively. Somebody, and I apologise for this expression, somebody messed up at corps level, these services, lawyers and other people like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have one more.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just follow-up on the same question. Did you see the date when that document you received on the 17th of March, 1993 was dated? Did you see when it was drafted, the date on when it was drafted?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, 1993 from the corps I received an order stating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know you've received that, and I'm asking you precisely about that order. What was the date of that order that you received?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gentlemen, now you are asking me to remember after all these years what had happened. To be quite frank, do you know how long it's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- how many years?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have come here to testify about things that happened many years ago. It was dated the 16th of March, 1993, so you got it the following day. So there was -- nobody messed up. You want it to come on the screen? We can bring it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 17th of April, as far as my memory serves me. The 17th of April from the corps, and there is a stamp, a stamp of receipt. If I think back now, there was this red stamp stating that it had been received from the corps, the 17th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am not talking about the date of receipt, I am talking about the drawing of making -- writing out that order. Can we please have it on the screen. What is the reference number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For the promotion itself, the 65 ter was 31996. And I think it might be P7122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No it's P7121.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, it says here very nicely the 17th of April, 1993, corps command. The red stamp, just as I said. My memory does serve me well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, just look at the top of that document. See the 16th of April --

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me. You asked me when I was informed. This is meritorious for me. The higher command did not contact us directly at all, the General Staff. We do not have that kind of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you please stop and listen. I haven't asked you when you received it. I have asked you what you know -- what is the date of the order? The date of the order is right at the top of the document there. Can you see that? It's not the 17th; it's the 16th. The day before you received it. You received it the following day on the 17th but it was drafted on the 16th. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that that is a matter for the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you see the date, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- yes, it's written there, the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You received it the following day according to the stamp down there. So it was just the following day.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're wrong. It wasn't the following day. It was registered in the corps on the following day. You see the stamp of the corps here. They wrote this on the 17th of April. I don't really understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did you receive it? When did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me way too much, aren't you? I mean, I don't even know when I received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, you've told us that you received it on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I have --

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask for what I said yesterday to be shown again. The corps placed this stamp here when they received it, and it's at the office there. And when a document arrives, it doesn't have to be handed out straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few follow-up questions in relation to what I earlier touched upon. Yesterday when you were attesting to your statement, you made a few changes. I have difficulties in understanding that, on the one hand side, you say, "I didn't know that I could make any changes, it was too late," and in court you made changes. You may remember that you were asked whether Muslims and Croats did not respond or -- then you said, "No, it was not the Muslims and the Croats but it was some Muslims and some Croats." So you changed your statement there. Now, why do you explain to us that you were not aware that anything could be changed, especially where there is something which was just not the truth anymore because you knew about the shelling of Hambarine? You say, "Well, I didn't know I could change it," and on other matters you did change your statement. That's difficult for us to understand. What then triggered the changes you made when you thought that you could make no changes. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't remember President Cehajic and later on I did remember, and things like that. Well, you will allow for the fact that I am 67 years old and my memory doesn't serve me that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What then triggered you to make such tiny little changes as Muslim changing to some Muslims; Croats changing into some Croats? We have -- we're trying to understand why on such details you made changes, and whereas on a matter, which may be far more of substance - that is, who shelled Hambarine - that you didn't make any changes?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain? What you said just now, some details concerning Muslims and Croats, those are not details for me. It was written there mistakenly, perhaps it was intentional, that these were pure units. It was just certain Muslims and certain Croats that refused mobilisation. I can tell you to this day who stayed on until the very end. Badnjevic, Ernest; I told you about him yesterday. He volunteered, went to Omarska, and then, from there, went to the VRS and stayed there until the end of the war. That is very important. The units were not pure. Believe me, that's the way it was until the end. As soon as I read this, I said that for the sake of these people, the Muslims and Croats who were in the army. It is wrong for that to stay on. I remembered Hambarine. I don't see what's bad about that, that I told you that it was Maric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you read about the shelling of Hambarine and when you read, "I don't know who participated in it, I don't know who ordered it," then you didn't think -- "but meanwhile I learned that it was the VRS so I should correct that as well."

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying in all sincerity that I didn't know. But then when I learned it, I said the head of artillery, Lieutenant Maric, and what's wrong with that? There are other details that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is our problem is the following. That when asked about why you didn't change your statement, you said, "Well, I didn't know that it was possible," and carefully looking at what you did is that you made changes. So apparently, or at least there is some potential contradiction, that you knew that you could change your statement, because you did it on some aspects, and at the same time you explain the Hambarine issue by telling us, "Well, I didn't know that I could change my statement," that is a -- that is difficult for us to understand and -- but if it is --

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was a slip of the tongue in the way I was expressing myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just briefly refer back to -- it was not yesterday but on the 9th of February, page 31375. You were asked by Mr. Lukic, and I quote: "And if I were to put to you the same questions today, would you substantially answer the same?" And then, indeed, you answered: "Yes, for the most part." Because that was very ambiguous, I asked on the next page: "When you asked if the witness," that was -- I was referring to Mr. Lukic, "if the witness would answer in the same way if the same questions were put to him, he said 'Yes, for the most part.' And what about the other part?" And that was then put to you. And your answer was: "When I said 'for the most part,' I meant that now I would provide much broader and more detailed and more complete explanations and answers than I did before, because I answered questions from my own standpoint as a professional, and I used a lot of terms and maybe jargon that may not be understandable to all." So that was your answer, but no clarification with respect to the issue we just discussed. I just wanted to put that on the record in all fairness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is hereby done. If you want to comment on it -- you explain not that "for the most part" meant that inaccuracies you would leave them apart. You just said, "I would give more details." When you said in your statement, "I don't know who shelled Hambarine," it's not a detail to now know. It's just you now do know, and that's a different answer to the same question. I leave it to that in view of the explanations you have given already. Mr. Traldi, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very briefly. Could we have 65 ter 32002.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, sir, Mr. Lukic asked about the Council for National Defence. Now, the members of it did have the authority to issue orders to the members of the organisations underneath them; right? For instance, Colonel Arsic had the authority to issue orders to subordinate units; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the operative part. Operative units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well -- so this is an order, the 17th of May, 1992, from Colonel Arsic on replenishment and unification of war units, and he says it's issued pursuant to an order by the 5th Corps commander and a conclusion reached at the Council for National Defence that we looked at in connection with ensuring unified command and control. And it's sent to the Serbian TO staff of the municipality of Prijedor. So in the course of implementing an order from his own superior command, the 5th Corps, Colonel Arsic issued an order to subordinate units implementing conclusions reached at that same meeting, the 15th of May, 1992 that Mr. Lukic showed you; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe -- because I don't have the right to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm confused by this, I really am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you have any objection, you may --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document is clear, "based on the order" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness remove his headphones for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, could you take off your earphones. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what I'm illustrating -- what I'd understood Mr. Lukic to be doing was calling into question the implementation of the conclusions reached at that session. What I'm illustrating is that Colonel Arsic not just because the decision was reached at that session but in the course of implementing an order from his own superior command, through his chain of command, which was consistent with that conclusion, issued an order implementing one of the other conclusions reached at that session which I'd discussed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, this was based on the order. We can mention something else but there was an order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it was just based on the order and if the other decision had nothing to do with that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it would not have been mentioned. That is -- it seems that we are now arguing rather than that -- if you have any objection against the question that Mr. Traldi put to the witness, you may object to the question but not by saying, "Look, the order is clear," because for Mr. Traldi apparently - and that's the dispute - you think it's clear, Mr. Traldi interprets it in a different way. Now, Mr. Traldi can ask questions about what happened, but you can't intervene by saying, "Well, the order is clear, so you shouldn't ask this question," unless there is a clear distortion of what the document says. Then the question would be misleading. The question, as phrased, may lead to some argument but is not misleading in itself. And, therefore, if you have any other objection against the question, you may raise it now and then we'll rule on that, already assuming that what you said was an objection to the question. And that's what your role is at this moment, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just if it satisfies Mr. Lukic's concern, I'm certainly not suggesting that the Council for National Defence was issuing an order to Colonel Arsic. He participated in that discussion and issued an order implementing a conclusion that was reached in a discussion he participated in that was consistent with another order he had reached through -- he had received through the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not challenge that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how we understood the question. Do you have any objections against the question, certainly after it being clarified, as Mr. Traldi did?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spent the whole case discussing this body and Crisis Staff, and I know for certain that this body could not order anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- you are giving evidence, Mr. Lukic, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Stakic case in the judgement of this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'll stop you there now. You say it's decided by this Tribunal. Is there any adjudicated fact you considered of such importance that you put it forward and you asked us to take judicial notice of that? Most likely not because it is a legal issue, and it's a legal issue which is debatable and therefore not fit for taking judicial notice of it, it not purely being a fact. I'm not aware of any fact related to that that you proposed for taking judicial notice of. If not, then whatever other Chambers said is not something that this Chamber would look at, and I take it that you are happy that we are not just taking all kind of information from other judgements where it has not been formally introduced in this case. Therefore, the argument that you know it and that other Chambers confirmed it is not something that we should consider at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- one second, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I already said to you that to the extent we had to understand your observations as an objection that it was denied. And if there is any other objection, not of the kind you raised but one in a technical sense, a serious objection to the question, you may raise it now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise -- you don't have anything else. Then, Mr. Traldi, we'll invite the witness to put his earphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just again, as we do to be pellucidly clear, what I'm illustrating, what I intend to illustrate, is that as a factual matter one of the conclusions was implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, what Colonel Arsic is doing in this order, pursuant to an order received through his chain of command, is issuing an order implementing the conclusion to put both TO staffs under the unified command of the Prijedor garrison; right?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Should I explain? This shows very nicely that the commander of the Serb staff - I was not the commander of the Serb staff of the TO of Prijedor, rather this one. When I said that decisions were mostly not being carried out, my thinking was right. Commander Arsic says very clearly all paramilitary units that are armed should be placed under the command - should be placed under the command - and they were not. I said that at the session. I've already told you about that, when the colonel was there, when we asked that armed people in Kozarac and Omarska should be placed within establishment and under the command. So what General Arsic ordered here was not carried out by Slobodan Kuruzovic. He was responsible for that. I don't know much about these units. And for me these are not units. Those people who did not serve the army, who did not have uniforms, they were paramilitaries and they were all over the place. I already told you about the Green Berets, some kind of volunteers, too, Serb volunteers, and what they did from all three sides. The command of my staff placed -- was placed under a different command. It seems you weren't listening the other day at all when I was speaking about this in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- refrain from making such statements. Any further questions, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, the Green Berets and -- or the people you refer to as Green Berets and armed people in Kozarac, measures were taken against them. They were attacked. The Serb paramilitary groups, against whom this order says "appropriate legal measures should be taken," no measures -- they were never attacked by the 43rd Brigade, were they?

utterances.speaker: RADE JAVORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. But they were not attacking the armed forces, whereas the Green Berets were. And the armed forces are within establishment and under the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32002 receives Exhibit number P7122, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have no other questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Javoric, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you - sometimes even more than that - and questions put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Thank you for having allowed me to expand on certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- may I be excused? I have to see the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I wanted to briefly give a statement in private session that will not take more than one minute. Of course you can leave, Mr. Lukic. But it could be that you would be interested what will be said in this one minute and, of course, after that, you are entirely free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, I hope to see you back soon. Meanwhile, is the Defence ready to call its next witness which would be Mr. Davidovic, if I'm well informed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. Mr. Nenad Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom -- oh, it's break time. Yes, yes. It's break time. It's good that there are always some assisting in repairing my mistakes. We take a break and will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we wait for the witness, there is one preliminary matter. There are two associated exhibits to the witness statement of this witness. Both have already been introduced into evidence, including D00676. And the English translation of the version that was introduced into evidence does not have two pages from the B/C/S original. We had advised everyone of that on October the 28th and had uploaded the full translation as 1D17-0229. But when Your Honours made the order two weeks subsequent to that date, it appears that the old translation was the one that was attached and therefore the English translation is not complete. So at this time I would ask Your Honours to please rule to have Madam Registrar replace the English translation with the one that I have just recited and then the two documents will match up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll -- in order not to make any mistakes, I'll literally quote you. We are talking about D676, which was admitted on the 10th of November. I do understand that a complete translation has been uploaded under number 1D17-0229. And you are inviting me to instruct Madam Registrar to replace the translation which is there at present by this new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perfect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you are hereby accordingly instructed to replace the existing translation by the one I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic. Mr. Davidovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Davidovic. Mr. Davidovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Doctor. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am Nenad Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to call up in e-court 65 ter number 1D1679.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I would direct your attention to the left-hand side of the screen in front of you, and I would ask you if you could tell us whose signature appears on the first page of this witness statement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now turn to the last page of the document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we also see a signature. Can you tell us whose signature is here?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the date that is recorded on this page, does it accord with your recollection of when you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, subsequent to signing this statement, did you have a chance to read the same in the Serb language to verify if there are any corrections needed to it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to now turn with you to page 4 in both languages, and paragraph 17 of your statement. Sir, what correction did you want to bring to our attention in regard to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that I attended one meeting. However, it should state that I participated in one debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what about this reference to Exhibit P0404, to what part of the paragraph does this document apply?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does the document that is listed, P0404, apply to your participation in one debate or to your role in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: About my contribution to the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to page 5 in English and page 6 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification, because it's not entirely clear to me. If you say you participated in one debate, was that in that one meeting you describe; or did you attend more meetings but participated only in one debate? That's not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I attended several meetings. I took the floor only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 5 in the English and page 6 in the Serbian and look at paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is titled as being in relation to the killings in Begici. Sir, what correction do you need to inform us about in relation to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know where Begici is, but I believe it's to do with Vrhpolje. If it has to do with Vrhpolje, then fine. But as for Begici, I really don't know even where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And apart from these corrections that we have gone through now this morning, do you consider the rest of your statement to be accurate as drafted?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you questions today based on the same topics as in the statement, would your answers to those questions be the same as are recorded in your written statement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth, does that mean that the answers as contained in your written statement are truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D1679 as the next public exhibit. Again, both of the associated exhibits have already been introduced through other means and therefore are not being sought for admission at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of them is a P exhibit; the other one is a D exhibit. Before we decide on the matter, could I again seek clarification. You say you do not know where Begici is. Nevertheless, we find in your statement that you said something about Begici, and you said, "Well, if that's Vrhpolje, then it's okay as far as I'm concerned." First of all, how -- do you have any explanation as how the word "Begici," where you say "I don't know where it is," ended up in your statement at all, which you signed a year ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally believe that Begici is a hamlet near Vrhpolje. That's what I personally believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you say "I don't know where it is," although you now say you believe to know where it is. But how you signed a year ago this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That means you have no -- your knowledge is such that you can't be sure. No, but how did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did the text in your statement -- I mean, if you don't know for sure where it is, nevertheless you are telling us about what happened there and you signed for that a year ago. Now, I'm wondering what happened that in your statement of one year ago the reference to Begici appears?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that there is a reference to Begici, but I don't know where Begici is exactly. I don't know its location, but I believe that it is close to Vrhpolje. That it is a hamlet up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you mention it during your interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I told the lawyer that I thought that it was there but that I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did you say "something happened in Begici but I don't know where it is," or was it put to you that something had happened in Begici and you then responded "I don't know exactly or for sure where that is"? Which of the two -- or if there is any other description of what happened, please tell us how it ended up in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was some killings there. I don't know who was killed and how they died. I was not sure where Begici was. I only heard about that. I was not present. I don't know what happened. But if Begici has to do with Vrhpolje, then Begici is a hamlet close to Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what do you know personally about what happened? But, again, you've still not answered my question: Who came up with the name "Begici"? Did you mention it or was it -- or were you told that something happened in Begici? How is it that it appears in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that somebody mentioned that, but I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now what do you know personally about what happened there? You were an eye-witness, you were not an eye-witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not an eye-witness. I was not in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where did you learn and how did you learn the details of what you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were rumours about an armed conflict in Vrhpolje, that there was casualties on both sides, and so on and so forth. I was not there. I was not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know who were killed in Begici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rumours had it that 13 Serb soldiers were killed. I don't know how many died on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, rumours tell you that 13 soldiers were killed and this then, as you describe it, was -- you considered this to be obviously a retaliation. Now, what did you know about the 13 soldiers being killed? Were you an eye-witness of that happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not an eye-witness. But I know that they hailed from the same territory, that they were all neighbours, relatives, friends, but I don't know. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you also say in your statement -- you describe in detail what happened to the Muslim that had killed the soldiers. You give details of that. Could you tell us what is the basis of your knowledge for those details, such as having Islamic marks on his clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that in town. I didn't see that personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the same for the copy of the Qur'an next to him. It's also that you heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see anything myself. I only heard things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From whom did you hear those details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In town. There were rumours about a man who had a Qur'an and Islamic insignia and that he killed 13 soldiers. I personally was not there. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you don't remember the person who told you this? It's just, you said -- well, there were rumours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a long time ago, 20 years ago. There were rumours. I really can't remember who could it have been who told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can have one clarification first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second. Yes, Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to understand the correction you are bringing to paragraph 26, is it your position that instead of saying "killings in Begici" it should read "killings in Vrhpolje"? And that the sentence should read: "The killings in Vrhpolje"? Is that the correction you want us to put on your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I don't have a clarification. That was the one I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you wanted to put a question to the witness to clarify a matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour has already asked the question I wanted to ask. So it's clarified. I now tender the document as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you tendered it already, and I then -- before deciding on it, that I put those questions to the witness. It was not, I think, that you had not tendered yet. But let's check in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, but it still has not yet been admitted, Your Honours. That's the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm aware of that. Yes. I misread when you said you don't have a clarification. That's clear. Madam Registrar, the number for this document -- there are no objections, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01679 receives Exhibit D897, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D897 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Davidovic -- I take it that, Mr. Ivetic, you first want to read a short summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you have further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll first listen to a summary of your evidence, Mr. Davidovic, and Mr. Ivetic will then have further questions for you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness was born in Sanski Most but completed his dental studies in Belgrade and also a specialisation at the military medical academy in Belgrade. He spent his entire career working in the health centre in Sanski Most. He was mobilised into the 6th Sana Brigade in June 1992 and stayed in the brigade as the chief of medical service. Prior to being so mobilised, he was engaged in the medical service of the Territorial Defence of Sanski Most. In Sanski Most, the Muslim SDA was arming the Muslims and established Green Beret units. One was active in the town itself; other units were formed in Vrhpolje, Trnovo, Hrustovo, and Kamengrad. Serbs believed the genocide that had been perpetrated against them in World War II was going to be repeated. There was almost no family in that area who had not had members killed by the Ustasha in World War II. The members of the Sana Brigade were often engaged in combat and suffered the most losses in the Gradacac area. After combat in Vrhpolje and Hrustovo, the witness was part of an asanacija or sanitisation activity to remove and document human and animal remains killed in combat. An investigative judge went along and the witness believes everything was documented. As regards medical treatment in Sanski Most, no one ever differentiated between patients based on their ethnicity. This was true even within the military medical service. As to specific incidents for Vrhpolje, the witness says that these crimes were committed by locals as retaliation of the killing of 13 soldiers from the area who had been killed by a Muslim combatant armed with a machine-gun, with the Qur'an, and wearing Islamic symbols on his clothing. The military commanders were trying to prevent revenge killings, but it was difficult to control the armed men whose children, relatives, and friends had perished. As to Skrljevita, the witness says that those crimes were committed by Dane Kajtez, who was not a member of the brigade, and that he was found guilty of those crimes by a judgement of the Bosnian court. That completes the summary. I would now like to turn to page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And focus on paragraph 9 of your statement. Here you talk of a book authored by a Muslim which provides details about how the SDA was arming Muslims. First of all, could you tell us anything more about the author of the book? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The author of the book is from Sanski Most. He is a writer. And he described the SDA organisation from the beginning to the end, from the founding meeting at the beginning of September, the Executive Board, the Main Board, people who were in charge of organising and expanding the SDA, how the SDA was armed. First the Green Berets were set up as well as the Patriotic League. In this document, he says that there are 300 armed fighters in Vrhpolje. It's their own document. There was one half of our brigade plus the town and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you to clarify. You say that was half of our brigade. How many soldiers did the 6th Sana Brigade have in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, before you ask that question, your previous question has not been answered. Who was the author?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe at line 13 it says he is a writer and he is from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: An author is a writer. Who was "he" is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he is indeed from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we all accept that the author of the book is the one who wrote the book and that in that respect he is a writer. Could we know who it is? Could you tell us who the author of the book was?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, could you tell us who authored the book? What's his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember as I sit here today. Kljucanin. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you get hold of the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was published only once. It had one edition in Sanski Most. People got hold of it. We made photocopies and then it was banned and never reprinted after that. I have the books. If you want me to, I can bring it with me tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you have the book but you don't know what the name of the author is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I can't be sure. I believe that his name is Kljucanin. I am not sure. I believe it's Kljucanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you know he's from Sanski Most. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that he's from Sanski Most. I am sure of that. Because of the name -- the family name, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say he bears a family name of a family which is known in Sanski Most and that made you conclude that he's from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you if you have the book itself or photocopies of the book in your possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up D676. I think we can at least clarify some of that by looking at -- I think it should be page 3 in English and page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the inside of the book cover, does this assist you as to the author who you have been talking about of this book?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Here we have the publisher, the editor-in-chief, Zilhad Kljucanin. I don't know whether the author is his brother Nihad. I am not sure. But we'll clarify that. Then you have other people. Mirzet Karabeg was a member of the SDA. Zilhad Kljucanin and Muhamed Lemes [phoen] is the former president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look down in the area that's boxed off that has information about the book that is entitled "It is a Crime to Forget a Crime: Sanski Most." It indicates Zilhad Kljucanin and a Hazim Akmadzic, first edition, Sanski Most, Sanski Most municipality. Does that -- is that the people that you have been talking about with the last name --

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These are the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "these are the people"? What kind of people are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people that wrote that. Zilhad Kljucanin, I am sure that he wrote that and that he is a writer. He lived in Sarajevo for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you look at the top of the page, you see there an entry, "Editorial board," and then five names appear, one of them Zilhad Kljucanin. It doesn't say anything about him being the writer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Editor-in-chief. That's what it says. Editor-in-chief, Zilhad Kljucanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And two lines below the name appears again as he was a member of the editorial board.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Editorial board, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see anything which indicates who, in fact, was the writer of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have it towards the end of the page, Zilhad Kljucanin, "It's a Crime to Forget a Crime," and Hazim Akmadzic, Sanski Most. So it's according to that. In my view, that means that they are the authors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have two authors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two authors, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we still have this page on the screen, I also note the name of Adil Draganovic as a member of the editorial board.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What position did Mr. Draganovic hold in Sanski Most before the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Adil Draganovic was president of the basic court in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What role or position did Mr. Draganovic have in Sanski Most following the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Following the war, he was president of the basic court yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of Mr. Draganovic's activities in Sanski Most following the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the Serb population left Sanski Most, time was needed for people to start going to their homes in Sanski Most. People did that at their own initiative. All of those who came to Sanski Most first had to report at the basic court at Adil Draganovic's, they had to give statements there. People told me that there were pressures there and that they provided false testimony and whatever. At any rate, you couldn't go into town. You couldn't go to your place of residence. You had to go to Adil, to the court to give a statement. All Serbs who came to visit their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now you say people told you about this. Could you tell us a bit more about the source of this information about the activities of Mr. Adil Draganovic in Sanski Most following the war? Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the ones who went there to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The source for your information of what was happening that they were being asked to sign statements subject to pressure and providing false testimony and whatever.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were my neighbours, and all the people who went never said, "No, I didn't go to see Adil." Everybody had to go to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could return to D897.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And page 3 in both languages. And paragraph 11 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you say that no one differentiated between patients based on their ethnicity. What about wounded enemy soldiers? Did anyone differentiate between them?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Differentiation on the basis of ethnic background? No. Health workers provided medical treatment to everyone, regardless of who it was that had been injured or had a health problem in any other way. All of them received care.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as in regards the health workers and medical staff themselves, were there any non-Serbs that remained to work in Sanski Most throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Savanda and Dr. Mirzet Halilovic, a surgeon. They worked with us throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the ethnicity of these two doctors that you have identified.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Halilovic was a neighbour of mine. He's a Muslim. And Savanda was a Palestinian, or something like that, married to a woman from Sanski Most who was a nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to the next page in the statement and look at paragraph 15 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, sir, you talk about the Crisis Staff President Nedjeljko Rasula and his command over the TO. First I want to ask you, what was the relationship of this TO vis-à-vis the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The VRS was not in Sanski Most at first when the Crisis Staff was formed. Professor Nedjeljko Rasula did head the Crisis Staff, and he was a man who wanted to have a say in everything and to have the decisive say in everything. He was that kind of person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you lay a foundation for the knowledge on which statements like "he was that kind of person who would have a decisive say in everything"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, how long prior to the war had you known Mr. Nedjeljko Rasula?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was Mr. Rasula prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: A high school teacher in Sanski Most. He taught the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your interaction with him prior to the war? How did you know him? Since you say you knew him since high school, how did you know him since high school? In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew him as a teacher, a home teacher. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And prior to the war, what type --

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war, too. Yes. I studied and then did my specialised training, and then I started working, and he always taught at the high school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how would you describe him before the war as to what kind of person he was in terms of the assessment you made earlier today about how he was at the Crisis Staff where you said he was decisive -- wanted to have a say in everything and have a decisive say in everything? How did he compare in the time-period before the war when you knew him?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was always that way. He was never a person who was in favour of compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in relation to the Crisis Staff, did it exist the entire duration of the war in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. The Crisis Staff started to work -- stopped working as soon as the municipal organs were established; the president, the Executive Council, and everything else that was there in the organisation. I think it was sometime in the month of July, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, how would you describe the interactions between Mr. Rasula and the brigade commander, Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Brigade commander and president of the Crisis Staff -- or, rather, the president of the municipality, they did co-operate, but there was no love lost between them. There was no love lost between them, but they did co-operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, looking at paragraph 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which you also have on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- you mention the SOS, Serbian Defence Forces. What was this formation? Was it a part of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. An organised group. The Serb Defence Forces, at first they listened to Rasula and later on I heard that they were renegades, that they did not obey him either, and Colonel Basara insisted that this unit be disbanded and attached to the 6th Sana Brigade. It was difficult but I think that he succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know how long the SOS was in existence in Sanski Most as a separate renegade formation?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that went on for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, 5 in the Serbian, and stay here in the English. I'd like to look at paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, here you are talking of the collection centres. And when you say in your statement "I know that people were beaten there" in relation to Betonirka, what is your precise knowledge and basis for this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I personally came along when a man who was detained in Betonirka was injured and then we sent him to the medical centre to provide medical assistance to him. I went and informed Colonel Anicic, who was head of the Territorial Defence, and I said that that happened, and he said that he would take all measures so that this would never happened again. And later on I did not hear of any other beatings and I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down slightly in speaking, Mr. Davidovic. And just a short follow-up question: Do I understand that you know only of one person that was injured in Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally know only of one and I intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you say you personally know only. Do you, perhaps not by personal knowledge, know of others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would have corrected your statement where it says "I know that the people were beaten there," which suggests that it's not one person was ever once beaten but "the people were beaten there." And now you tell us that you only know from direct knowledge and from indirect knowledge only of one person that has been beaten there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A person I saw and a person for whom I intervened. That is the only person I saw, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now what did you learn from others about people being beaten in Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I immediately cautioned Colonel Anicic so that he could stop this beating of people, because he was in charge of Territorial Defence, and he promised that he would do his very best so that this would not happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not clear to me. You say you cautioned Colonel Anicic so that he could stop this beating of people, which again suggests that it was not just one person but there had more been beaten. But at the same time, you tell us that you were aware only of one person that had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you that I know of one person who I saw personally. I saw what I saw. Now what I did not see, I cannot make any claims if I did not see something. I saw one man who had been beaten up and he was given medical assistance. Now, whether there were other people, that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, your statement is full of claims on matters you have not seen but you present for a fact. We dealt with that extensively earlier where you said it was only rumours. Now what I'm asking you, is it your evidence that you saw only one person that had been beaten, you reported that, and you did not hear or learn in any other way about others being beaten in Betonirka? Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know only of one injured person who had been beaten up; the person I saw. As for all the rest, I cannot make any claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is did you hear, and I'll ask you then in what way, did you hear about other people having been beaten which you may not have seen yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't -- I mean, I really don't know. I really cannot give an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why can't you answer the question whether you heard about other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear. I mean, had I heard, I certainly would have reacted. I certainly would have reacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, apparently you are in a position to answer the question you did not hear of other people being beaten here, which clarifies --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear. I did not hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which then clarifies what we find in your statement, which suggests otherwise. But we have heard your testimony now. But, Mr. Ivetic, could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just ask for one clarification. When did that happen, the beating of this one man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's a question from me to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was May or June. May or June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.
