utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One follow-up question. A short one. You state that a physician was present in collection centres every day. Could you tell us who went to the collection centres every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A physician went every day. A physician and a nurse. The lady doctor who was in charge of the gym is Dr. Brankica Lazic-Karadzic. And she had the task of going every morning and examining patients, providing therapy to them, and I don't think that this collection centre remained for very long. I think it was disbanded very quickly. But for as long as it was there, a doctor did go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you are talking in your statement about collection centre centres, in the plural. Which collection centre were you referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew of Betonirka. I knew of the sports hall, and later on Krings. I was not there, but I heard that it was Krings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the same doctor went to all these three correction centres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. To the hall. A doctor went to the hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who went to Betonirka on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A medical technician went to Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not a physician, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A person with a secondary school education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your statement, we read: "A physician was present in collection centres," the plural, "every day." So that's not true, if I understand you well. Certainly not for Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe that is wrongly stated, "in all centres," but at the sports hall there was a physician every day. And in Betonirka, there was a medical technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the third one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I was already at the brigade. I was chief of medical corps there and I stayed there until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. So, therefore, you have no knowledge about any medical assistance provided in Krings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you have used already 30 minutes. But if you have one or two more questions for the witness, and preferably about facts he has knowledge about, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, our proofing statement had asked for 45 minutes for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. You've asked for more time. But what I -- the remainder of what I said still applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, did any non-Serbs stay in Sanski Most for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my assessment, about 3.000 loyal Muslims remained in Sanski Most throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the VRS or the Sanski Most authorities undertake any hostile actions against these 3.000 loyal Muslims who remained in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer so that the interpreters could interpret.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: They protected the population as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when somebody else, apart from the VRS or the Sanski Most authorities, undertook hostile action or mistreated these Muslims who had remained loyal and who had stayed in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us your knowledge of when that happened.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That happened in 1995, when Arkan and his units arrived in Sanski Most. He mistreated the Muslim population and the Serb population. He carried out lootings in town. He tied people to trees in parks. He shaved the hair off their heads. He sent people to the front line whimsically. He went to these Muslim settlements looting. He could do this because our units were all out defending the town, so no Serb, Croat, or Muslim was protected from Arkan. From us at the medical centre, he took an ambulance for two reclining patients, and he looted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did he have permission to take the ambulance from the medical centre that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not have permission and he didn't ask anyone for permission. He did that on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now my last area of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On page 5 in English and page 6 in the Serb of your statement, and paragraph 24 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you talk about the fact that not many Serbs live in Sanski Most today. Can you tell us the circumstances of how and when Serbs left Sanski Most during the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs left Sanski Most during one afternoon and half of the night. The entire population left, whoever was able to leave, because BH units assaulted Sanski Most. Before that, Sanski Most was bombed. It was shelled. And I think -- I think that they came from the NATO Rapid Reaction Force. It wasn't the Muslims that were doing the bombing and shelling. We fled during the afternoon and night. Only old and frail people stayed in Sanski Most, and most of them were killed then. There was a centre, a collection centre, near the cinema in Sanski Most where Serbs had been detained, and those who got out confirmed that. However, after the war, only a few hundred Serbs stayed in Sanski Most. And out of that figure, there aren't any children or young people. Wahhabis appeared in Sanski Most. They married local girls, local Muslim girls, and they live in Sanski Most. Quite a few of them do. Otherwise, the economic situation is bad in Sanski Most. Nothing is working in Sanski Most. Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could back up and have just one final question, sir. You indicated that you think that the shells that were bombing Sanski Most when the Serbs were leaving came from the NATO Rapid Reaction Force. Can you please tell us the bases for your belief that it was these forces which were shelling Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps before doing so to tell us what day this happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- could you first give the day? You said in the afternoon. So in a very short period of time the Serbs left. Could -- do you remember what day that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two days after Dayton. It was a Tuesday. I think it was the 10th or 12th. The 10th, must have been the 10th. The 10th, must have been the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] October. Month of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what makes you remember that this was two days after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know that Sanski Most and Mrkonjic are the two towns that fell after Dayton. That the cease-fire had been signed, and two days after that Sanski Most and Mrkonjic Grad fell. That that is how I remember. And I know it was a Tuesday because I had left my native town and that remains deeply etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dayton, if you refer to Dayton, you are referring to the Dayton Accord to be concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was some cease-fire that had been signed. Cease-fire. And after that -- now, was it Dayton or was it something else? Anyway, something had been signed. And after that, only two towns fell; that is, Sanski Most and Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least we have now a time-frame. Mr. Ivetic, any further questions in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the original question I'd asked, what was the bases for his belief that the NATO Rapid Reaction Forces were the ones that had shelled Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it was them because when a bomb is thrown by the Muslim army, we see the moment when it's fired and when it hits its target. However, the bombs that fell over Sanski Most on that day, those shells, we did not hear when they were fired. We only heard them when they hit their targets. That's why I believe that they did it. This is very indicative. In town we would hear if a shell was fired from a 5-kilometre or a 10-kilometre distance, but on that occasion we did not hear that moment and that was not normal. That's why I think it was them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That answers all my questions. I thank you on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of the team for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I also see we are at the time for the break, Your Honours. But that ends my direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take a break, Judge Fluegge has one follow-up question, and I may have one or two as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know that it was NATO Rapid Reaction Force, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was nobody else there. If a shell was fired from somewhere around Kljuc, we heard that. If, on the other hand, it came from somewhere on the Adriatic we couldn't hear that, and there was no other forces deployed along the Adriatic. I believe that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I put this question to you because the Defence has reported to us that you have referred to another unit during the proofing before you entered the courtroom. We see in a note we received from the Defence that it was UNPROFOR Rapid Reaction Forces. What do you exactly know about it? UNPROFOR or NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know. I wouldn't know which unit. But it was none of our units; Muslim, Croat, or Serbs. It was either UNPROFOR or rapid reaction forces. One or the other. I don't know for a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem is that you state something which you then later say you don't know. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask you a few questions about paragraph 31 of your statement. Could it be shown to the witness. And that's the next page in B/C/S. Yes. A few questions in relation to the killings that took place in Skrljevita. First of all, who was killed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Skrljevita is a village which was inhabited mostly by Croats. 99 per cent of the population were Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, my question was who was killed there. How many persons were killed, who were they, how were they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know any details. I know there were rumours about Dane Kajtez, who was not a member of the brigade and his uncle was the brigade commander, that he was behind that. Croats were those who were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Where your statement says: "I know they were committed by Danilusko Kajtez, also known as Dane Chetnik," are you explaining now that that is what you learned through rumours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That man was tried and found guilty and he's serving a prison sentence for those murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you at this moment. Unless you want to say that you learned about him being the perpetrator only when he was tried. And, by the way, you said a few lines ago that you learned that by rumours, and I'm asking you now -- let me just see. "I know that there were rumours about Dane Kajtez." How do you know that he was the one who committed those murders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The town was rife with rumours about that. Everybody spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I asked you. You say you knew it through rumours. Now, you say he was never a member of the 6th Sana Brigade. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I was a member of that brigade. I did not see him in a single unit, in a single company, in a single battalion, nowhere on any of the front lines. I didn't see him. If he had been a member, I'm sure that our paths would have crossed during the three or four years of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say, "Since I did not see him over those years," which you would expect would have happened if he would have been a member of the 6th Sana Brigade, you concluded that he never was a member of the 6th Sana Brigade; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I am sure that he was not a member of the 6th Sana Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I want to know how you know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is impossible that I did not come across him anywhere during the three or four years. I inspected all of the battalions when they lined up before going on a front line. I attended all those occasions, and I never saw him. I didn't see him on any of the front lines in any of the lineups. Territorially, he would have been a member of the 3rd Battalion but he was never with them. He never was employed -- deployed with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just theoretically, let's just assume that he would have been a member for two weeks in a unit which you did not visit during those two weeks. Your explanation as how you knew for sure that he never was doesn't apply any further, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, on the one hand; however, on the other hand, you are not right. If I, for example, was not on the front line on one occasion, and he was there on that occasion, it is impossible that our paths did not cross for four years. It is impossible that our paths would have never crossed. If I remember the lists of the brigade members correctly, I did not see his name on any of those lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. He was found guilty, you said, by a final judgement of the court. Which court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The BiH court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was that judgement delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four, five years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well after the war, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And he's serving a sentence now, if I do understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you that, that last -- that he's now in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard from people from Sanski Most. The brigade commander is his uncle, and he told them that he was serving a sentence in Foca -- actually, his uncle told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. That's a clear source of knowledge. You'll be cross-examined after the break. But I think that Judge Moloto -- perhaps I should have taken the break already, but Judge Moloto has just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question. Do you know whether he was brought to justice by the military authorities immediately after or during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that he was remanded in custody already during the war, and then the civilian authorities or, rather, civilian courts tried him and found him guilty after the war, and that he was investigated and he was remanded in custody by a military authority or a military court during the war when that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And one very short question: Do you remember for how long he was then remanded during the war by the military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know exactly, although my cousin was a military court judge. Still, I don't know. I don't know how much time he spent in custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at half past 12.00. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, just in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding. The Judges have put quite a lot of questions to the witness. Mainly, they were aimed at a better understanding of the witness's testimony; that is, whether he speaks from his own knowledge or whether it's -- he is relying on other sources rather than that we want to revisit the substance matter which is in the statement. So there may not be a -- of course, I leave it to the parties, but -- Mr. Ivetic, or Mr. Jeremy, we are not saying -- not suggesting that you should go into the substance of all what the witness said. Where we asked questions where we were mainly focusing on what is the source of knowledge of the witness, and not necessarily that we are primarily interested in the substance and the truth of what he may have heard by rumours or from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You find Mr. Jeremy to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement in paragraph 13, you indicate that during the war you spent almost the -- almost all the time in the field, and you indicate you stayed the longest in the Gradacac war theater. Now during 1992, it's correct, is it not, that the times that you were in Gradacac were in August and September; yes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were also in Bosanski Brod in September; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were again in Gradacac in March 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I spent most of the time in Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you say in your statement that in Gradacac you would have ten dead on average per shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, did you keep a record of these numbers of dead persons, numbers of wounded persons during the time you were in those theatres?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to move topic now and discuss your attendance at Crisis Staff meetings, which you refer to in paragraph 15 to 18 of your statement and which you've mentioned already today. Now, during the war period, how many Crisis Staff meetings do you estimate that you attended? Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number. I would say approximately five, six times, and I was in charge of the medical service there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Five or six times. Now, I'd like to take a look at the Crisis Staff meeting that you refer to in your statement in paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P404 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So firstly, you recognise this document, sir. It's the minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting you attended on the 30th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we see that there is a list of 12 persons. Number one is a reference to Nedjeljko Rasula, who you mention in your statement and you've mentioned today. We read that he: "Leads and organises the work of the Crisis Staff and co-ordinates and harmonises the work of our Crisis Staff with the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina?" Further down, we see number 9, Nenad Davidovic, in charge of municipal medical services. So that's obviously a reference to yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we see that below this list of names --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we go to the second page in the B/C/S, please. Or, sorry, the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see that there are two points circled; number 1 and number 2. Focusing on number 2, we see that there is a reference to: "A long-term solution is to be found for the problem of refugees from the Mahala area as well as the Muslims and Croats who are not loyal to the constitution and the laws of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." The sentence goes on. I won't read it. The next sentence reads: "Also make contact with the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina regarding implementation of the idea on resettlement of the population." So that role would primarily have fallen to Nedjeljko Rasula as did the principal liaison between the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most and the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now you would keep a record of the Crisis Staff meetings that you attended; yes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You would keep a record of those meetings in your diary; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take a look at your diary from this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 19777.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So referring you to the left side of the screen, sir, we see the front page of a document that states: "Diary of Dr. Davidovic, Nenad, member of the Sanski Most SDS Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this page is not mine. I didn't type anything on it. If it says Nenad Davidovic, a member of the SDS Crisis Staff, I have to tell you that I was never an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at a few entries in this diary, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 24 of the diary, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what I'm going to, sir, is the record -- the notes of the Crisis Staff meeting that we have just looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In fact, it's page 25, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. So we see here the 30th of May, 1992. And we see a reference to KS at the top of the page. KS, what does that indicate, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it indicates the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, in view of one of the previous answer, could we first verify that this is what -- this is the witness's diary? Because he earlier said something about the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes, Your Honour, I was trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, sir, do you -- I can ask you now, do you recognise your handwriting that we see here of this record of the Crisis Staff that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it, but the first page is not mine. The first page that you showed me before is not mine. Somebody added it to the document, somebody else typed on that page, erroneously I must say, but the rest is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's understood. Now, we see at the bottom of this page, we see a reference to "President should work on long-term issues of the Muslims and Croats in the territory of the municipal," and that's a reference to Rasula. It's the -- that -- it's the same reference that we saw in the --

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- minutes we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, here we see the list of the persons appointed as members of the Crisis Staff, and we see number 8, Nenad, medical corps. That's a reference to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go back to the previous page, please, in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, drawing your attention again to the bottom of the page where we -- I've already read, that the "President should work on the long-term issues of the Muslims and Croats in the territory of the municipality," now my question is this: The basic position of the Serb authorities in Sanski Most at this time was that those persons who were considered not loyal to the Serbian authorities were to be expelled together with their families; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The unloyal ones, yes. But the loyal ones should be left and protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And by "unloyal ones," could you explain what exactly you mean?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the referendum when leaving Yugoslavia, there was a split among the peoples, the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, and that's where it all started. All of it started from there. There were people, Muslims, who voted in our referendum, the Serb referendum, for staying in Yugoslavia. They came dressed in their best clothes, they came to the cinema, and they voted publicly to stay on in Yugoslavia. However, we were outvoted. People who were in favour of staying in Yugoslavia turned out to be loyal and they did not organise themselves and arm themselves. For the most part, it was the SDA that led the Muslim people, organised them, made their numbers larger, equipped units with weaponry while establishing them. Already at the outset when the conflict started, people themselves asked to leave. They felt unsafe, they were afraid of war, fighting, death.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- if I understand correctly, those persons who voted to stay in, those Muslims -- those non-Serbs who voted to stay in Yugoslavia you considered to be loyal, and those who did not you considered to be unloyal and -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. Mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it was those unloyal persons who the Serb authorities in Sanski Most intended to expel from Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some left on their own, and some left sort of out of fear from fighting. People who had relatives went out voluntarily and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- already in the very beginning, the place got pretty empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- I'm not asking you about all the reasons why the people left. I'm asking you about the intention of the Serbian authorities and whether it was their intention to expel those non-Serbs who did not vote to stay in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy. Before we continue, I'd like to seek clarification, which is: Witness, the following was put to you, whether you consider to be unloyal those persons who voted to stay in -- those non-Serbs who voted to stay in Yugoslavia you considered to be loyal, and those who did not you considered to be unloyal. Your answer was "mostly." What is not correct in that description? Where do you make any reservation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly means that there were people in favour of leaving Yugoslavia but were still loyal, who accepted the new authorities in Sanski Most and who did not take part in arming and the establishment of units of the SDA. There were people like that, too, but at the referendum they voted in favour of leaving Yugoslavia. However, they did not side with the radicals. They did not join SDA units. It wasn't a massive thing, but there were people like that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In connection with this, let's take a look at another page in your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And while we're getting there, I can tell you that there is no date connected to this particular entry, but it appears between a dated entry on the 21st of May and another entry -- a dated entry on the 25th. So it's -- the assumption is this date -- this entry is dated between that period. So we see that there is a meeting. We see the heading: "Disarming the population." And there are a few hyphenated points. If I go down to the -- refer you to the fifth one, we read: "- everyone resisting Serbian authorities will be expelled together with their families." Now, this is a reference to the non-Serb population in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. If he's going to read it, he should read the entirety of the submission for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Da." [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- context because the next section also deals with the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I think you can read it item by item. But if you would consider it better, Mr. Jeremy, you may follow the suggestion and not leave it to Mr. Ivetic to deal with the matter in re-examination. I leave it to you. Therefore, the objection is denied but you certainly will give it some thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I would put on the record that the witness answered the question by saying "da" which was not interpreted and didn't appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which will be verified through the audio, of course. Mr. Ivetic, I don't know whether you heard it as well or whether you have any trouble --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He did. It was in the middle of what I was saying, so I don't know whether he was saying "da" to the question or to what I was saying, so I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You agree that he said "da" but you still have to interpret what that means in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Then can I also -- would I then also -- could I conclude that the parties have no -- that the "da" does not appear on the transcript, that the parties are not divided on that matter, that the witness say "da"?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I heard the witness say "da" as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If everyone does, then the parties can -- apart from what it means, agree that the witness said "da"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, just -- I would also draw your attention to the bullet below, the point below, which states that: "- all extremists will be expelled from the municipality, while the authorities guarantee safety to all loyal citizens." And I think that concurs with the point that you made in relation to the previous entry; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, it was the loyal population that was given protection. As for extremists, no. No guarantees to them. Extremists were those who were organising and arming the people, the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it's correct, is it not, that regardless of your definition of extremists, then their families were also no longer welcome in Sanski Most and they were also to be expelled; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part. For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And looking at this entry now, do you recall whether it was yourself referring to the expelling of persons resisting Serbian authorities with their families, or was it somebody else at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was not in charge of that area, so I was not involved. I was in charge of organising medical services.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It was Nedjeljko Rasula who was in charge of that area; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly Nedjeljko. And there were people who assessed the security situation in the municipality, who were in charge of that, and who had information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just find some clarity, please. Mr. Davidovic, the heading of this little topic is "Meeting!" Is it correct to assume that these points are decisions made by that meeting? Decisions taken in the meeting by the people who were in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proposals. Proposals for decisions. And then decisions were made in a narrower circle, the president and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just to clarify an answer you gave earlier. When Mr. Jeremy asked you: "Everyone resisting Serbian authorities will be expelled together with their families." Somewhere you said: "Da." Were you responding to that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you the question. Is it one of the proposals of the meeting that everyone resisting Serbian authorities would be expelled together with their families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I have one follow-up question in this respect as well. In that line, reference is made to "everyone resisting Serbian authorities." Now, in the line after that, reference is made to "all extremists" that will be expelled. Now, what's the difference between someone resisting Serbian authorities and an extremist? When are you an extremist, when are you someone who resists Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that extremists are those who are prepared to fight. Armed combat extremists. Not those who are unloyal. Those who are unloyal do not obey. So that's the difference. So extremists are those who are prepared for an armed fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So extremists are those who are willing or even already taking up arms, whereas everyone resisting Serbian authorities are just those who disagree with the Serb rule which applied at that point in time. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well understood. You understood it well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why would those who opposed Serbian rule to be expelled? Isn't it a democratic right to be active, to change the laws and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was almost a state of war. Almost a state of war. And in -- and one could not really speak about a democracy. One could not. For the most part, I think that people who put up armed resistance were the ones that were targeted. Armed resistance. Now, whether they agreed with the authorities or not, that is a different matter. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this squarely contradicts your previous answers. I asked you what is the difference between those resisting and extremists. You said extremists are those who are willing to take up arms. Others may have been unhappy with the situation but are not within that category. My question therefore is: If you have advocated to stay -- to leave Yugoslavia and therefore not being in favour of the new Serb rule without willing to take up arms, if that category -- my question was why that category should be expelled together with their families, where they just politically disagreed with the present situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally would not have expelled them. I personally. If they do not agree politically. Now, who made this decision to expel, that's a different matter. But extremists, I'd expel them too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it's clear that in this entry in your diary, apparently it was proposed that those who were not willing to take up arms but disagreed should be expelled as well, together with their families. Apart from your personal opinion about the matter, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this was the position. The position was that they should be expelled, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to look at another entry in your diary a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Again, it's undated but it -- I can tell you it appears before -- immediately before an entry on the 23rd of May, 1992. Here we see the Croat -- the heading is Crisis Staff meeting. We see number 1, "Conclusion," and a number of -- a list of points below that. So, sir, to be clear, these are -- the points below "Conclusion," these are the conclusions that were adopted by the Crisis Staff at this particular meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, halfway down the list of those conclusions that were adopted at this meeting, we see a reference to Colonel Basara, decree, calling them to hand in their weapons. So just to be clear, this is a reference to the Colonel Basara who was a member of the 6th Sana Brigade in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 6th Sana Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And where we see "calling them to hand in their weapons," the "them" refers to Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Serbs in Sanski Most were not asked to hand in their weapons, were they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: All of those who had no papers and weapons, they were duty-bound to hand over weapons irrespective of whether they were Serb, Croat, or Muslim. So it has to do with illegal weapons. Muslims did not have their weapons taken away from them either if they had the right documents for these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So provided Croats and Muslims in Sanski Most had the correct documentation, then it's your position that they could retain their weapons throughout the war period; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You understood that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Another clarification. Mr. Davidovic, when Mr. Jeremy asked you about that bullet point where Colonel Basara's name appears and asked you what the "them" referred to, you agreed that it referred to the Croats and the Muslims. Now, I ask you about the next bullet point under that. Sir, it says: "Expelled from these areas forever." Is it still the Muslims and the Croats who are to be expelled forever? Is it the same "them" that were in the upper bullet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see that here on this paper that is in front of me in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Colonel Basara's bullet point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I wouldn't know who this pertains to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could it be it pertains perhaps to the people who resisted the Serbian authorities and those who were extremists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be that it's them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, these references to disarming, expulsion, and later in this list of items we see a reference to certificates to leave, these -- this reflects the planning for what followed in the weeks and months in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Do repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly perhaps I'll just draw your attention to the fact that the third point up from the bottom refers to certificates to leave AR, autonomous region. I take this to refer to the Autonomous Region of Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And my question was that this -- this reference to disarming, decrees to persons to hand in their weapons, from being expelled from these areas forever, to certificates to leave, this reflects the planning that was going on in the Crisis Staff for what would follow in the following weeks and months in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I could not assert that. I don't see how I would formulate that. I don't know whether it was organised -- I mean, what you are saying is organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, we see that you are involved in these meetings where plans are being made to disarm people, to expel people, certificates to leave are being discussed. So -- I mean, that's not simply abstract planning on a hypothetical basis. That's planning for what would -- for what you intended to follow in Sanski Most and for what, indeed, did follow in the following months; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I wouldn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may ask the questions, then. Were people subsequently disarmed after these decisions were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for most part, yes, people did surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And were these people expelled after these decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I know they were disarmed, and what happened then I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, earlier today I asked you how many -- or you were asked how many Crisis Staff meetings you -- you attended. I asked you the question and you indicated five or six. Now, this diary is -- the entries are from the 5th of May, 1992 to the 3rd of March, 1993. And even for that period, which is less than a year, there are over 30 entries that indicate that the entry relates to a meeting of the Crisis Staff. Does that reflect your recollection that, in fact, you attended five times as many Crisis Staff meetings in less than a year?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot claim that it was five times. Perhaps it's a bit more than that. I don't think it was 30. Maybe the Territorial Defence Staff meetings, something like that. But Crisis Staff, no. Not that many. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't propose to go through each of those 30 entries now. Let's go to another entry, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please look at page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this is another Crisis Staff meeting on the 25th of May, 1992. So, sir, we see the heading -- we see the date, 25th of May, 1992. We see Crisis Staff. We see a reference to protection of important buildings - done. Number two, Crisis Staff constant session. We see a reference to organise two prisons, and below that the names Papric and Krunic. Now, Papric is a reference to Mladen Papric; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And he was responsible for the -- for Betonirka; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And Krunic is a reference to Milorad Krunic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And he was responsible for the detention facility at Hasan Kikic school; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know about the Hasan Kikic school. But we can agree that, at least in respect of Betonirka, that's one of the two prisons that point number 3 is suggesting should be organised; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, below that reference to the prison, we see a reference to bring in Adil Draganovic. You mentioned that you knew him and you've mentioned your knowledge of him today. We also see a number of persons should be arrested, Redzo Kurbegovic. And I also see a reference to Ismet Jakupovic. That's the person that you mentioned earlier today who you guessed might have written the book that we were discussing --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- correct? I think you said it could have been Ismet or his brother.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not mention Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I can get the transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can assist. The -- and I did not want to rise to make an objection, but the -- other names were used. And I just had it and I just lost it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give a page and line reference, that would be appreciated, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to get to, Your Honours. That would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Must be somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- from page 37 through page 39, and at page 38 and 39, I believe -- 39, line 1, gives the name of the individual which might assist counsel. So it's page 39 throughout -- well, actually, page 38, lines 25, through page 39, line 22. Line 2, pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, that does assist. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. I've got the wrong name. It's actually Nihad Kljucanic [sic] who you referred to earlier today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kljucanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the transcript tells us as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask you, was there a Kljucanin and a Kljucanic? Are these two different people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kljucanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, looking at your entry, it -- does that refer to a Nihad Kljucanin?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: What entry? What reference do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on the upper half of the handwritten version. A bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the underlined part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, there is a name that is underlined on the screen before you, written in your hand. What is that name?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nihad Kljucanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, apparently the English transcription is not accurate. Mr. Ivetic, everyone agrees that the original is about Nihad Kljucanin as the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I note that there are other typos on this page as well, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's then -- there is no dispute about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So these are a list. These -- this list of persons to be arrested or brought in, they are some of the leading non-Serbs in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The reference to civilians for exchange, that's a reference to non-Serb civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The reference to attack at 6.00 a.m., that refers to an attack to be carried out the following day; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. Not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, the reference to "do not arrest with weapons," that means take no prisoners if armed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can't arrest people with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But if they had -- if they were holding weapons, then they were to be killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: If they put up armed resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go to an entry in the diary of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, I take it that you're moving to a different page and I rather have one more question. This Mr. Kljucanin who you said was one of the authors of the book, was he an extremist? And let me clarify: Was he someone who had taken up arms or where you had information that he would take up arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know that, no. I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, his arrest is ordered here. Do you know why he should be arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It was security officers who made suggestions as to who should be brought in based on their assessments of the people in the field and on their estimate as to who might be dangerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said that these were all prominent non-Serbs which are listed here for -- to be arrested. Do you know of any of these names - that is, Mr. Kurbegovic or Mr. Karaleg or Mr. Jakupovic or any of those names - do you have any knowledge, specific knowledge, about why they should be arrested apart from referring to what security organ's assessment might have been, but have you any knowledge about why these specific persons were to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know that. What I see before me, a list of those people, they were all connected with the SDA, the Executive Board, the Main Board, the army, and so on and so forth. And specifically why people are brought in, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So being connected with the SDA Executive Board would be a sufficient reason to arrest someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that it was so strongly connected with the Executive Board. It was more about arming and people who were involved in that, in the arming of other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But when I asked you whether -- why you had -- whether you had any knowledge as why they would have to be arrested, you referred to such links rather than to suggest that it was because of arming that they should be arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we didn't understand each other. If somebody was a member of the SDA, it doesn't mean that he was necessarily against -- or, rather, in favour of armed rebellion. Not everybody was. But there was a group of people in charge of arming, and they were affiliated with the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But for the one person you are aware of, that's Mr. Kljucanin, you do not know whether he was -- you do have no information as whether he would be an extremist and he would take up arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Page 81, line 15, after the Main Board. I heard "arming," and I asked my colleague in the B/C/S, the word used apparently was "arming," not "army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In my view, it was at least unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's perhaps the best answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll -- you mean the word -- the English word used by interpreters? We could easily verify.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes the word, indeed, was "arming."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreter has clarified that it was "arming." Thank you for assisting in making the transcript as accurate as possible. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, the non-Serb civilians for exchange referred to here, now the intention was to capture these non-Serb civilians, keep them as prisoner, and then later exchange them; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where were they brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see a reference there to civilians for exchange. You confirmed that this is a reference to non-Serb civilians. And my question is this: The intention was to capture non-Serb civilians, hold them as prisoner, and then later exchange them; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. The civilians which were either exchanged or left the municipality voluntarily were never brought in or arrested. They volunteered to leave by bus. They were not brought in or sent to some collection centres, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we have this entry number 3: "Organise two prisons." We've got some text below it. The text refers to the leading Muslim and non-Serb persons in the municipality. Below that, "Do not arrest with weapons," and then we've got the reference to "Civilians for exchange." It's your position that that doesn't refer to taking into custody or imprisoning those civilians but just being ready for when they came to you and asked for an exchange, then you would facilitate that. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is well understood. People who wanted to leave Sanski Most volunteered. They did not have to be brought in. No collection centres had to be organised for them and they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So this entry doesn't anticipate the capture of civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, one clarifying question. If civilians could voluntarily move out if they wished to do so, why would they wait for being exchanged? I mean, what -- why would they? They could leave if they wished to leave. What does "exchange" mean under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They volunteered to leave Sanski Most; civilians, that is. They took buses and they went in the direction of those municipalities which were controlled by Muslims, whereas people who arrived from the territories controlled by Muslims who were of Serb origin arrived in Sanski Most. There were times when the number of the population in Sanski Most doubled. One still didn't leave, the others had already arrived pending the departure of the former.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're describing a situation where some people move out and other people move in. Now, the word "exchange" suggests that you could move out only if others could move in, that it was arranged for rather than if I want to leave I leave, if someone wants to travel in, you travel in. So my question is: What does "exchange" mean in this context at all if everyone was free to move in and out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In factual terms, there was no exchange. It was impossible to carry out any exchanges. There was nobody to exchange people for. If from Bosanska Krupa people arrived, 3.000 of them in Sanski Most, then 5.000 people leave Sanski Most at the same time. This is not an exchange. It's never meant to be an exchange. An exchange is when you bring people to a certain place where another group of people is waiting and you exchange one group for the other. And this is not an exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree with me that the word "exchange" is used here, and I inform you that the Chamber has received evidence that exchanges of the kind as you describe did happen - I'm not specifically referring to Sanski Most at this moment - but that those exchanges were happening, sometimes even with larger number of people. Any comment on the use of the word, also in view the evidence this Chamber has received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, this term, "exchange," is wrong. It doesn't function well. It does not reflect the factual situation. If somebody leaves a municipality and if somebody else comes to that municipality, this is not an exchange. This is perhaps just a misfortunate use of words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We've heard your explanation. Mr. Jeremy, please proceed. We have to take a break, as a matter of fact. Could you give us an indication, Mr. Jeremy, as to how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I estimated two hours. I think that I will be less than that but I don't anticipate concluding today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that's clear to us. Witness, you may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Yes, perhaps I briefly deal with the following matter: Associated exhibits remaining from the testimony of GRM130. On the 27th of November of last year, the Chamber addressed the Defence with regard to the number of associated exhibits through Witness GRM130 and reiterated its preference for having such exhibits used with and tendered through witnesses in court. This can be found at transcript page 28949. However, no additional submissions were made, nor were the exhibits used with the witness in court. The Chamber would therefore like to clarify with the Defence its intention with regards to the 13 remaining associated exhibits tendered with Witness GRM130; in particular, whether it has considered withdrawing any of the remaining exhibits. And I can imagine that you could not immediately respond to this but we would like to receive a response not -- perhaps tomorrow, that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see, Mr. Stojanovic, you are nodding yes. We would like to receive a response tomorrow. Mr. Davidovic, Mr. Jeremy will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can we please have P3294 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, while this is coming up, I can tell you that it's the diary of Mr. Rasula, and I'll be referring you to page 57 in the English and page 40 in the B/C/S. And this particular diary entry is on the same date as the entry that we just looked at in your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the right-hand side of the page in the B/C/S, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see that -- I refer you to the 25th of May, 1992. We see that this is a Crisis Staff meeting. We see, number 1: Information on security of important features. Going down the list, number 4, pre-empting enemy operations. We see arrest of leaders. And we see: "Detention facilities (Miladin Papric and Mico Krunic)." Those are the two names you mentioned in connection with the entry in your diary. At the bottom of the page, we see item 4, various persons are to be taken into custody. So, sir, this is the same -- this entry is relating to the same meeting that we just looked at in your diary; correct? Mr. Davidovic, should I repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My question is whether the entry that we see here in Mr. Rasula's diary is minutes relating to the same meeting that we just looked at in your diary.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in the English and the B/C/S, please. We'll need to go to the left side on the B/C/S. Sorry, could we go to page 40 in the B/C/S. This is page 40. Could we scroll over to the right side, then. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, focusing your attention at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, and we're looking at the top of the page in the English: "Tuesday, at 6-7 o'clock, the operation begins. "- the fighting will not stop until they surrender. "- take no prisoners if armed." And the final bullet: "- captured civilians to be used for exchanges." So this entry clearly reflects the factual situation. That is, that civilians were to be captured, imprisoned, and used for exchanges; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if civilians are captured, where they will be accommodated and what other population they will be exchanged for. I'm really not clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, regardless of whether you're clear of whether those civilians will be kept, can we agree that the intention is clearly to capture those civilians and exchange them?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I see in this document. But where will they accommodate them if they capture them and who will they exchange them for? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question please, Mr. Jeremy. The witness asks himself questions as to how to understand it and apparently is not able to give any information. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Let's go to the next entry, please, in Mr. Rasula's diary. That's page 58 in the English and 41 in the B/C/S. So we're on the right page in the English. If we can look at the left side. Sorry, could we scroll over to the other side in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see this is a Crisis Staff meeting. It's dated the 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next -- if we can scroll over to the right side in the B/C/S, please. And if we could go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see your name, sir, there, at the bottom of the page in the English: "Nenad Davidovic - what we are doing was imposed on us." So, sir, you were present at this particular meeting; correct? That's a reference to you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we scroll over to the left side on the B/C/S, please, and go back one page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could just go back one page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, we see that, number 1, there is a reference to Major Veljko Brajic, talking about himself, his personality, and character. Then a few lines down -- ten lines down or so, we see: "In future work, we must make sure ..." And then number a): "That prisoners of war are to be taken over from MUP/Ministry of the Interior/, held overnight, and the most extreme among them isolated and punished so as not to walk this earth." So this Major Brajic suggesting that the most extreme prisoners of war are to be isolated and not walk this earth, that was the chief of staff of the 6th Brigade in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you personally came into contact with non-Serbs that were arrested during the disarming operations in Sanski Most during this period; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not with all of them. I did with some.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I am not suggesting you came into contact with every one of them, sir. Could we see -- could we now go back to your diary, and I'd like to look at an entry in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: 65 ter 19777, please. And if we could go to page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see that this is a meeting on the 28th of May, 1992. So it's a couple of days after the entry that we've just looked at. We see that number 2 there is a reference to "Doctors' stand on refugee issue," and I want to focus your attention on number 8, Mehmed Alagic. And we see a reference to: "Mehmed Alagic - identity card and money. "with me. "handed over/to crime?/" So, sir, where we see "with me," it's correct that Mehmed Alagic was with you for a period of time on the 28th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is not correct. I never saw Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can you explain why you would -- why at that time you would have made a note of him in your diary and suggested that he's with you and handed over to somebody?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not in contact at all with Mehmed Alagic because he's a colleague of mine, professionally speaking. I would have remembered that for sure, had I been with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Was he considered an extremist in Sanski Most at this time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you consider him an extremist?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the answer would rather be yes than no, because he was under the strong influence of Faik Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see he's the eighth name on a list of persons below the heading "Doctors' stand on refugee issue." That reference to "Doctor," is that a reference to you? Is it a reference to your stand on refugee issues?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In point number 2, we see: "Doctors' stand on refugee issue," and my question is whether "Doctor" is a reference to yourself, Dr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. All doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you said you knew Mehmed Alagic and you say that he was a colleague, also a fellow doctor. So you also know that three days after the entry that we see here in your diary, Mehmed Alagic was found dead on the Sanski Most city bridge. You knew that; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that, that he was killed soon afterwards. It was May or June, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we, as the last document today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, this is your diary, isn't it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you intended to write down when you wrote "identity card and money with me handed over/to"? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't remember that that was handed over to me and that I had that. Maybe yes, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Another follow-up question. Mr. Davidovic, the third line on the top, with the number 2, could you please read that as it is written there? Read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean this: Seric, Muhamed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no. On top of the page where we find now the first -- and please read that one line under number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Doctors' stand on refugee issue." Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Exactly. Is that a plural or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All doctors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but could we invite the parties to agree linguistically on whether it says stand on refugee issue by the doctor, of a doctor, or whether it's a reference to a plurality of doctors? Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear what the witness said now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness should not talk unless he's asked something. But I'll now ask you: Is that the stand on refugee issues of a doctor or is it of -- linguistically does it refer to doctors in the plural, because it is translated to us as "doctors' stand on refugee issues," which could be both singular and plural, if I am --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Plural, plural, the position of all doctors. Because medical care had to be provided to refugees in the territory of the municipality; that is to say, it is the plural. It is the stand or position taken by all doctors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your explanation. We'll have this linguistically verified. Then there is a list of nine persons. What does that list stand for? I mean, why did you list nine persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not say. I don't even know who all these people are. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you wrote their names down and you even referred to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then next question, please, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that we're nearly at the end of the day. I was going to look at a document also in connection with this, but it will take a few minutes, so I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is a few minutes? Is that less than -- is that five or less, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Five or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five or less. Then I am looking at the booth whether -- and I see that, as always, we get the full co-operation from those assisting us, which is again highly appreciated. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 17364.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this is a report on the clearing up of the terrain in the town of Mahala dated the 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see that this is a report on the field inspection in the suburb of Mahala. We see that it's dated the 31st of May, 1992. And I want to focus your attention on point number 4 at the bottom of each -- the page in each language. We read: "The body of Dr. Mehmed Alagic was found on the bridge over the Sana River (the city bridge), following information by Sanski Most SJB duty ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we go over the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "... service. The body was identified, taken to 'Susnjar' Cemetery and buried under number 8 (in the second row)." Sir, this man was in your -- is listed in your diary in an entry a couple of days earlier. You say in your statement that you were involved in sanitation activities. Did you -- did you --

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would first wait for the question. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Is it your position that you were not aware that Dr. Mehmed Alagic died on this date even though you were entering his name in your diary two days prior?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that I was not with Dr. Alagic and that I had not seen him at all. I personally. When he was killed, I heard that he had been killed and buried. I did not have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did that knowledge have any particular significance for you when you heard about him being killed given that you wrote his name down in your own diary two days prior to his death and indicated that he was with you and handed over to somebody?

utterances.speaker: NENAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't with me. Mehmed Alagic was not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17364 receives Exhibit P7123, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Those were your questions, Mr. Jeremy? Witness, we'll adjourn for the day, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.30, in this same courtroom. Before you leave the courtroom, I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 12th of February, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
